Law Society calls for better legal aid provisions in family justice reform

Published on

12/11/2026

by

  • Ella Fincken
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 3:05
Instaread

As stakeholders eagerly await publication of the government’s delayed family justice strategy, the Law Society continues its push for substantive improvements to legal aid.

The Law Society of England and Wales has called on the UK government to ensure that its highly anticipated family justice strategy includes improvements to legal aid provision that ensure tangible support for individuals navigating family breakdowns.

The demand follows Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State Jake Richards MP’s confirmation in parliamentary questions this week (10 November) that the government will introduce a new type of order equipped with legal aid to allow representation for individuals “without [them] having to venture into their own personal finances”.

Richards also confirmed a child-focused model will be rolled out across the country by 2029, with the family justice strategy – a document setting out “systemwide actions” to reduce delays and demand, support family court users, and achieve earlier resolutions for children – to be published in “due course”.

Law Society president Brett Dixon said in a statement: “If the government is serious about its commitment to halving violence against women and girls, the family justice strategy must set out how the government will support its proposals.”

He stressed that improvements to legal aid provision will “ensure that the availability of legal aid to those going through family breakdown is more than just theoretical”.

While confirming the introduction of new legal aid-backed orders, Richards emphasised that a key priority was also making “the family court system work much more efficiently”, pointing to the number of delays and countless hearings facing victims trying to protect their families.

Dixon said the Law Society supports reforms intended to “improve the experience of families and children through the justice system” while making clear that “legal aid should ensure we can all be supported during some of the most difficult moments in our lives”.

“For too long survivors of domestic abuse have been caught between a rock and a hard place of either not being able to afford a lawyer or not qualifying for legal aid,” Dixon added. “This leaves them with impossible choices such as going to court on their own, taking on debts or even staying with their abuser.”

Delayed publication

Proposals for a family justice strategy followed fervent calls for reform from regulators, the judiciary and members of the public concerned about excessive delays, backlogs and governmental inaction. A report published by the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) in September 2025, Improving family court services for children, recommended that the Ministry of Justice and Department for Education publish a data and evidence strategy by April 2026.

In a July 2026 letter to the PAC, Jo Farrar, permanent secretary of the Ministry of Justice, said the Ministry had taken the reluctant decision to once again extend the timetable for the strategy, which had already been pushed back in March, and is now expected to be published by the end of November 2026.

Dixon is now calling for rapid action, urging the government to “publish the strategy” and “commit to much greater investment in the justice system”.
